text: Step 3 of the investigation plan: reading the actual execution plan for the exact query Lesson 4 identified as the top resource consumer. In SSMS, turn on Include Actual Execution Plan, Ctrl+M, before running it — the actual plan includes real row counts from this specific run, which matters because estimated-versus-actual divergence is itself a clue.

Three things to check, in order. Cost percentage: every operator shows a cost relative to the whole query, summing to 100%, and the highest percentage is where the optimizer thinks the time is going. Arrow thickness: thicker means more rows flowing between operators, and a thick arrow feeding a small final result is a red flag. And operator name: a scan versus a seek means something specific about how the data was actually retrieved.

For Billing's invoice query, the plan shows one dominant operator: a Clustered Index Scan on dbo dot Invoices, at roughly 90% of total cost, feeding a thick arrow into a Sort for the ORDER BY. Hovering that arrow shows the scan reading every row across every patient, just to find the handful belonging to one PatientID.

That's backwards. A query asking for one patient's invoices is reading the entire table to find them, then sorting whatever matched. Lesson 6 confirms exactly why: there's no index that lets the optimizer seek directly to a given PatientID.

This also matches Billing's exact symptom. A full scan costs roughly the same amount of work no matter which patient is looked up, and that cost only grows as the table grows — which explains why this screen gets slower over time, and worst during the morning when many clerks run the same query at once.
